name: Smart Contract
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Code That Carries Out Its Own Instructions
lesson.summary: A smart contract is a program stored on a blockchain that automatically executes predefined logic when triggered by a transaction, allowing agreements to be enforced by code rather than by a trusted intermediary.
lesson.body:
The term smart contract predates blockchains themselves. Computer scientist Nick Szabo described the underlying idea in the 1990s, imagining agreements whose terms could be automatically enforced by software rather than by courts or intermediaries, using a vending machine as his classic illustration: insert the right input and the machine mechanically guarantees the correct output, with no need to trust the machine's operator in the moment of the exchange. Blockchains gave this idea a practical home, because they provide exactly the kind of tamper-resistant, shared execution environment that makes automatic enforcement credible to strangers who do not trust each other.

A smart contract, in modern usage, is simply a program deployed to a blockchain, with its own address, that runs specific logic whenever it receives a transaction. This is where the connection to the underlying blockchain definition matters most: because the ledger is an append-only, replicated record that every node independently verifies, a smart contract's code and its resulting state changes become part of that same tamper-evident history. And it connects to transactions specifically because a transaction is the trigger mechanism: sending a transaction to a contract's address, often carrying some data describing which function to call and with what arguments, is what causes the contract's code to actually run.

Execution has to be deterministic, meaning every node processing the same transaction against the same contract state must arrive at exactly the same result, otherwise the network could not agree on the resulting ledger. This requirement shapes how smart contract platforms are built. Ethereum, the most widely used general-purpose smart contract platform, runs contract code inside a constrained virtual machine, and charges a computational cost, called gas, for every operation performed, which prevents a contract from looping forever and stalling the entire network's ability to process new transactions.

A simple concrete example illustrates the mechanics well: an escrow contract could hold funds sent by a buyer, and release them to a seller only once both parties send a transaction confirming that delivery occurred, or refund the buyer automatically if a deadline passes without confirmation. Nobody at a bank or a legal office needs to authorize the release, the contract's code enforces the agreed logic directly, and the outcome is visible and verifiable to anyone examining the blockchain.

It is worth being careful about what the term does and does not imply. A smart contract is not necessarily smart in any meaningful sense, and it is not automatically a legally binding contract in the traditional sense either, those are separate questions involving separate bodies of law. It is also not autonomous in the way that phrase can suggest: a smart contract does nothing on its own, it only ever responds to transactions sent to it, and it has no built-in way to reach outside the blockchain to check real-world facts, a limitation significant enough that it defines an entire separate problem worth understanding on its own.
